# Fossils in Everyday Speech

Language is full of dead things that still move.

Take the word "salary." It comes from the Latin *salarium*, which is linked to salt. The popular story is that Roman soldiers were paid in salt. Historians doubt that neat version, and the more likely story is that money was given to buy salt, or that salt was simply an emblem of what a person needed to live. But the word carries the idea across two thousand years. Every time you complain about your pay, you're invoking a mineral that most of us now buy for a few dollars and never think about.

Or take "muscle," from the Latin *musculus*, "little mouse." Someone looked at a flexing bicep and saw a mouse running beneath the skin. Nobody thinks of rodents when they go to the gym, but the image is still sitting in the word.

I find this moving because it means nobody is ever really speaking only in the present. When you say "I'm *disappointed*," you are, at a buried level, saying you've been removed from an appointment, an office you expected to hold. When you say something is "*sinister*," you're echoing the Latin word for "left," a sign of the old suspicion of left-handedness. We are all constantly quoting people we'll never know, whose metaphors got worn smooth by use until they became plain nouns and verbs.

Metaphors die in a particular way. At first, calling a flexing arm a little mouse is a joke, an unexpected leap. Then it's a common phrase, then just the word. The surprise gets used up, but the leap remains, hidden in the structure. Almost all of language is like this: a graveyard of former daring.

It makes me think that the boundary between poetry and ordinary speech is only a matter of time. Poetry is metaphor that still has its pulse. Ordinary speech is poetry that has been walked on for centuries until it became a path. Someone had to make the first bold claim that time was money, that arguments were wars, that ideas could be grasped. Now we say "I see your point" without noticing that we've claimed thought is a kind of vision.

I wonder what's being coined right now that will become invisible. "Download" is already nearly there. "Viral" is halfway between a joke and a plain description. In a thousand years, someone might trace a word for spreading popularity back to a disease, and feel the same small vertigo I feel over the mouse in the muscle.

The past isn't only in museums. It is in the mouth, in every sentence, doing quiet work. We inherit not just words but the imaginations of everyone who used them before us, and each time we speak, we lend our own small leaps to whoever comes next.
